title: Circuit Breaker Credits: The Best Tools for Property Tax Affordability (Samms & Johnson, ITEP, 9 Nov 2026)

verdict: ENRICH objections/lvt-hurts-asset-rich-cash-poor.md (primary: add a defined circuit-breaker clause under 'The Response' item 2, ITEP as origin of its own characterisations only, state tallies B-claim, anchored to Lincoln); secondary light ENRICH events/proposition-13.md and places/kentucky.md; NEW concepts/property-tax-circuit-breaker.md recommended (short, Tier 1 Lincoln/state-agency anchored); NO enrich to research/cwc-distributional-impacts-lvt.md (no ITEP link: its flat refundable credit is not a circuit breaker; at most a see-also). Not a REJECT: scanner's relevance claim holds, but ITEP must not be cited as support.
claim_grade: Source tier: ITEP is a non-profit research and advocacy tax-policy think-tank (self-described 'non-profit, non-partisan'; PDF p.25), so Tier 2 under EDITORIAL 4c, judged the same way as the Tax Foundation entry in sources/audit/people-tiers.json (ITEP and the Samms/Johnson names are not listed there; rubric applied). Origin/proponent only, never support. Grades: B for ITEP's state tallies and programme classification (own analysis of statutes and forms, internally inconsistent in places, see uncertainties); C for ITEP's normative design recommendations and its judgement that circuit breakers are the 'best tools' and caps 'tend to favor wealthier people'; A only for official programme parameters once checked at the state agency (e.g. Minnesota refund eligibility ceiling $142,490, Minnesota Revenue page, matches ITEP Appendix B). Tier 1 anchors: Lincoln Institute of Land Policy (listed Tier 1 in people-tiers.json) for the definition, typology, counts and the cap/exemption critique, graded A/B as institutional research; state revenue agencies for programme facts, A.
content_summary: DEFINITION (PDF p.2, p.4-5): circuit breakers 'prevent a property tax overload by crediting back property taxes that go beyond a certain share of income'; 'under most circuit breaker programs, when a property tax bill exceeds a certain percentage of a taxpayer's income, the circuit breaker reduces property taxes in excess of this level.' Threshold-style is the most common type, delivered as a credit through the income or property tax system (p.5). ITEP adopts the Lincoln definition for non-threshold types: 'direct property tax relief to households ... increases as household income declines' (p.5, endnote 7). Example: West Virginia credit for property tax above 4 per cent of income, max $1,000, income limit $45,180 single / $61,320 married in 2024 (p.5). Idaho: $1,500 credit below $15,750 income in 2026 declining to $250 at $39,130, no explicit threshold (p.5).

STATE COUNTS (Key Findings p.2; p.6; Appendix A p.15-16): '29 states and the District of Columbia' have a circuit breaker (as of 2025; p.6); 14 plus DC use the threshold approach, 15 other forms; 'the remaining 21 states' have at least one other income-limited relief but no circuit breaker because they 'do not factor in the amount of property taxes paid' (p.2, p.6). Seniors-only: Key Findings say '19 out of 29' with 'the other 10 states and D.C.' covering non-seniors; body p.10 says '19 of 30' and 'Eleven states' cover non-seniors; Appendix A count row reads non-seniors 14/30 and seniors 30/30. Renters: Key Findings '20 out of 29 and D.C.'; body p.10 '21 of 30'; Appendix A renters-seniors 21/30, non-senior renters 8/30. So scanner's '19 of 29' and '20 of 29 plus DC' are the Key Findings wording; the body and appendix use a 30-jurisdiction base (29 states plus DC) and the numerators differ by one at most; the appendix non-senior count (14) does not reconcile with either 10+DC or 11.

CLASSIFICATION OF BORDERLINE CASES (p.5, p.6, endnotes 5, 7, 9; Appendix A note): since 2023 ITEP uses an expansive Lincoln-style definition (earlier ITEP publications counted only threshold programmes: endnote 9); 'other circuit breakers' are credits, rebates or exemptions whose value rises as income falls (Fig.1 note). Programmes giving the same relief to everyone below an income ceiling (flat-dollar homestead exemptions, deferrals, assessment limits with an income test) are 'not as carefully targeted' and are NOT counted (p.5). Hawai'i is counted although it has no state credit, because counties run circuit breakers (Honolulu, Maui, Kauai; Appendix A footnote). Nebraska's 'Homestead Exemption' and Washington's senior exemptions appear in the list (Appendix A-C), i.e. exemption-form programmes with income-graded benefits are counted. A table note says non-senior status counts only if broadly available, not for veterans, disabled people, surviving spouses.

DESIGN FEATURES (p.10-13): extend to all ages; include renters 'by treating a share of rent as a proxy for the property taxes embedded within it' (p.10; ITEP gives no percentage; the Lincoln 2010 article says states most commonly use 20 per cent and the Lincoln 2018 table lists 0.2 for DC); set an income ceiling above poverty level, citing states above $50,000: CT, DC, HI, ME, MD, MA, MI, MN, MT, NE, NJ, ND, VT, WV (p.11); benefit cap: most programmes cap annual relief at $200-$1,500; Minnesota homeowner cap $3,480 in 2025, Vermont combined cap $8,000; Nebraska covers the whole bill; set caps so a poverty-level household in a modest home pays no more of income than high-income households (p.11); index income limits and the maximum credit to CPI-U (p.11); threshold 'typically in the single digits', can be flat or vary by income; WV 4 per cent, Massachusetts 10 per cent; since the average high-income household pays no more than 2-3 per cent of income in property tax, a similar threshold is suggested for low- and middle-income households (p.12); allow ITIN filers (CT, MD, MN, NJ, DC; Colorado an alternate ID number) (p.12); administer through the income tax with a standalone-rebate option for non-filers; outreach, simplification, partial automation by data matching (p.13). No phase-out schedule is prescribed beyond Idaho's declining credit example and the Lincoln-style sliding scales; ITEP names 'phase-outs' only implicitly.

UPTAKE LIMIT (p.13): 'The principal drawback of circuit breakers is that they generally reach only those taxpayers who actively apply for them annually, whereas broader homestead exemption programs are often granted after a single application'; in some states 'many, or even most, eligible taxpayers are unaware'. No participation-rate figure is given for any state.

HOUSING COST FIGURE (p.3): 'About one in three U.S. households pays more than 30 percent of their monthly income for housing. This includes a quarter of all homeowners and half of all renters.' NO citation, endnote or source named in the PDF or page (endnote 1 on that page is the ITEP 'Who Pays?' 2024 study for the 4.4 per cent figure, not for this). Likely the Census ACS / Harvard JCHS cost-burden series but that is not stated, so the source cannot be attributed from this report. Also p.3: poorest 20 per cent pay 4.4 per cent of income in property taxes (ITEP 'Who Pays?', Jan 2024).

CIRCUIT BREAKERS VS EXEMPTIONS AND CAPS (p.3, p.14): both flaws of homestead exemptions, rate caps and assessment-growth caps: poor targeting and high cost to local governments (p.3). Homestead exemptions give the same benefit to all owners regardless of need; a flat-dollar exemption gives a $200,000 home the same benefit as a $20 million home; percentage exemptions are 'even less equitable, as high-value homes receive the largest benefits' (p.14). Assessment caps 'tend to favor wealthier people living in high-value homes that are appreciating quickly in value'; young families seeking a first home 'fare particularly poorly because artificially holding down the property tax bills of long-time homeowners pushes more of the responsibility for funding local services onto new buyers' (p.14). Supported by ITEP's own 2011 primers (endnotes 23-24), not new evidence. Cost: circuit breakers cost 0.03 per cent (Washington) to 9 per cent (Vermont) of property tax collections; average benefit $100-$2,000; federal EITC average $2,894 in 2025 (p.7). The claim that circuit breakers are 'in many cases, less expensive' is asserted, not shown for any state (p.14).

STATE DOLLAR FIGURES: Appendix C (FY2022, ITEP analysis of Census of Governments and state data, p.20-21): Minnesota homeowner refund 5.56 per cent of property tax collections, average $1,129, 494,627 claims; Minnesota renter credit 2.15 per cent, $731, 295,520 claims; Vermont 8.86 per cent, $1,609, 116,469 claims; Maine 1.34 per cent, $397, 119,000 claims; Montana PTAP 0.84 per cent, $843, 21,527 claims; Michigan 2.54 per cent, other fields n/a; DC 1.34 per cent, $1,064, 37,470 claims; Pennsylvania $473, 405,493 claims; Nebraska 2.67 per cent, $2,369. Appendix B (2026 income ceilings): Michigan $71,500; Minnesota homeowner $142,490, renter $77,570; Maine $63,750 single/$101,250 joint; Vermont $115,400; Montana PTAP $29,037 single/$38,917 joint; DC $66,000 under 70/$90,000 over 70. Appendix D thresholds: Michigan 3.20 per cent; Minnesota 12 per cent; Maine 4; Vermont up to 3; DC up to 5; Montana (elderly credit) up to 5; Wisconsin 8.785; Pennsylvania 15 (Philadelphia, Scranton, Pittsburgh only); Oklahoma 1; Maryland up to 9. Minnesota decile chart (Fig.3, p.9, from the Minnesota Dept of Revenue 2026 Tax Incidence Study): property tax after circuit breaker 5.8 per cent of income in the first decile, 2.5 in the second and third, about 3.0/2.9/2.9 in the 4th-6th, 2.6 in 7th-8th, 2.0 in the ninth, 1.2 in the tenth (decile mapping of bar labels is from extracted text and should be checked against the PDF figure before quoting); ITEP says the property tax remains regressive at the top and would need 'a progressive tax on high-value homes' (p.10). Local examples: Maui $8,200 max credit, 2 per cent threshold, income under $126,000; Melrose MA senior circuit breaker matches 100 per cent of the state credit (p.8).

APPENDICES: present. A (type and beneficiary groups, p.15-16), B (programme names and 2026 income ceilings, p.17-19), C (cost share, average credit, claims, FY2022, p.20-21), D (threshold rates, p.22). Sources: ITEP analysis of state forms, statutes and agency websites plus the Lincoln/George Washington Institute 'Significant Features of the Property Tax' database (2024 information).

LINCOLN COMPARISON: Lincoln's own definition (Bowman et al. 2009, 'Definitions of Circuit Breaker' box in chapter 3 and chapter 1 text; Lincoln 2010 article): circuit breakers are 'programs that provide benefits directly to taxpayers, with benefits increasing as claimants' incomes decline'; income-targeted exemptions or credits with a flat benefit below a ceiling are excluded because they lack 'the necessary inverse relationship between income and tax relief amounts'. Lincoln 2009 counted 33 states plus DC for 2008 (Hawai'i not among them; 16 states with none) and noted the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities counted only 18 because it counted threshold formulas only. Lincoln's 2018 summary table lists 30 states plus DC (AZ CO CT HI IA ID KS MA MD ME MI MN MO MT NC ND NE NH NJ NM NY OK PA RI SD UT VT WA WI WV, plus DC), i.e. ITEP's 2026 list is the same minus North Carolina, so ITEP's 29+DC is consistent with Lincoln's database lineage rather than an independent count; ITEP's inclusion of Nebraska's homestead exemption (which Lincoln's 2018 table also lists, so the choice is inherited) and Hawai'i's county programmes is a broad application of the Lincoln definition. Lincoln's 2009 typology: threshold, sliding-scale, hybrid and quasi circuit breakers (ITEP folds sliding-scale, quasi and hybrid into 'other circuit breakers'; its 15 non-threshold count cannot be checked against Lincoln's current database). Lincoln 2010 recommendations match ITEP's (all ages, renters, higher ceilings, multiple thresholds, reliable state funding); additionally: relief 'treated as an entitlement', most commonly 20 per cent of rent deemed to be property tax, Maryland multiple-threshold example, New York STAR case (20.1 per cent of NY homeowners paid over 10 per cent of income after STAR; 2006 ACS). Lincoln also says (2010) assessment limits 'are among the least effective, least equitable, and least efficient strategies' (quoting Haveman and Sexton 2008) and that fixed-dollar homestead exemptions 'do a poor job of targeting'; so ITEP's cap critique is a restatement of Lincoln's, and should be cited to Lincoln.

OFFICIAL PROGRAMME ANCHOR (Minnesota Revenue, fetched): Homeowner's Homestead Credit Refund regular refund requires 2025 household income below $142,490 and ownership and occupation on 2 January 2026; the special refund requires a net property tax increase of more than 12 per cent and at least $100; the refund is based on 'your income and property taxes'; subtractions for dependents, age 65 or over, retirement contributions, disability; a 2025 law change raised the 2025 homeowner refund by nearly 15 per cent; renters now claim the Renter's Credit on the income tax return from 2024. Matches ITEP's $142,490. Michigan Treasury page: HTTP 403, not retrieved; Michigan figures ($71,500 ceiling; 3.2 per cent threshold) remain ITEP-only here (Lincoln 2018 table lists a 3.2 per cent single threshold and a $60,000 ceiling for 2018, so the threshold is corroborated and the ceiling is a later update).
existing_wiki_coverage: Corpus digest has no page on circuit breakers, ITEP, or the Lincoln database; no concepts/ page (concepts/ has 90-odd pages incl. land-value-tax, tax-capitalization; none on property-tax relief). 'Circuit breaker' appears in only four wiki pages, not six: objections/lvt-hurts-asset-rich-cash-poor.md (undefined, one list item), events/proposition-13.md (one clause), places/kentucky.md (one parenthetical), and research/fox-liscow-love-tax-business-rents.md (a different sense: a metaphor for taxing the entity directly, so not related). The cwc page mentions 'deferral/circuit-breaker mechanisms' once, in its Design-sensitive bullet. Scanner's 'at least six pages' premise is therefore wrong. ITEP is cited nowhere (grep of itep.org / Institute on Taxation: no wiki hits); Lincoln Institute is already cited (Prop 13 [15], Gorey explainer, 21 Oct 2026). EXACT ANCHORS: (1) objections/lvt-hurts-asset-rich-cash-poor.md, 'The Response' list: '2. **Circuit breakers.** Caps tying the tax to a share of income protect low-income owners.' (Note: 'Caps' here is loose: a circuit breaker is a credit or refund of the excess, not a cap on the bill; ENRICH should replace with the defined mechanism. The page's Limits section contains the Pigou/CWC 43 per cent passage and the Net Assessment 'fully handled by deferral and phase-in' which a verified count and the take-up caveat would qualify.) Proposed ENRICH wording, impersonal: circuit breakers refund property tax above a set share of household income, taxpayers must claim them each year, and a tally of 29 states plus DC (ITEP, 2026, which adopts the Lincoln Institute's wider definition) is B-claim; renters covered by deeming a share of rent (most commonly 20 per cent per Lincoln) to be tax. (2) events/proposition-13.md, sentence in 'The 2026 Revolt Wave': 'The explainer ranks assessment limits of the Proposition 13 kind as "one of the most problematic" responses, illustrating with two Los Angeles houses of equal value paying $5,212 and $11,172, and prefers circuit breakers, deferrals, moderate homestead exemptions and truth-in-taxation laws.' Next sentence: 'Its one remark on land is the efficiency point that the part of the tax falling on unimproved land does not distort behaviour because "the supply of land can't be increased or reduced in response to a tax"; it does not discuss land value taxation as a response.[15]'. Proposed ENRICH: one sentence after 'truth-in-taxation laws.' defining a circuit breaker (credit when property tax exceeds a set share of income) and attributing to ITEP (Samms & Johnson, 9 Nov 2026) its judgement that assessment caps favour owners of fast-appreciating high-value homes and shift costs to new buyers, as an advocacy think-tank's characterisation, with Lincoln (2010, quoting Haveman and Sexton 2008) as the Tier 1 anchor. The Texas/Georgia rollback sentence is a truth-in-taxation point and needs no change. (3) places/kentucky.md: '...and administrative modernization of the county Property Valuation Administrator assessment cycle as alternatives that target aid to residents genuinely unable to pay without departing from fair-cash-value assessment or cutting revenue to schools and local services.[2]' and the parenthetical '(a refund when a property tax bill exceeds a set share of household income, used in 29 states)'. ITEP independently gives 29 states plus DC (Kentucky not among them: Appendix A lists no Kentucky; Lincoln 2009 listed Kentucky among 16 states with none), so the KCEP '29 states' matches ITEP's count excluding DC; ENRICH: add that Kentucky has no state circuit breaker (ITEP App. A; Lincoln 2009 note) -- B-claim until the Lincoln database or Kentucky Department of Revenue is read; also note KCEP's 12-state deferral count has no ITEP counterpart. (4) research/cwc-distributional-impacts-lvt.md, line 65: '- **Design-sensitive.** The headline result ... Other Georgist proposals pair LVT with a [citizen's dividend](/wiki/citizens-dividend/) or with deferral/circuit-breaker mechanisms (see [the asset-rich, cash-poor objection](/wiki/lvt-hurts-asset-rich-cash-poor/)) rather than an income-tax bracket change, and would likely show different incidence.' Recommendation: no change to claims; at most link the circuit-breaker term to the new concepts page, since a circuit breaker is an income-tested, tax-linked refund while CWC's $12,700 credit is a flat per-household refundable credit unrelated to tax paid, which is the distinction ITEP itself draws (flat benefits below an income ceiling are not circuit breakers, p.5).
uncertainties: NEW concepts page: WARRANTED but short. Reasons: the term is used undefined on three relevant pages, the objection page's current wording ('Caps tying the tax to a share of income') is imprecise, and a definition plus typology (threshold, sliding-scale, quasi, hybrid), renter treatment, take-up weakness and the contrast with caps/exemptions/deferral is reusable. Tier 1 anchors: Bowman, Kenyon, Langley & Paquin (2009), Lincoln Institute Policy Focus Report PF019, openly served as PDF (definition p.7; chapter 3 types; chapter 5 pitfalls; 2008 count of 33 states plus DC); Kenyon, Langley & Paquin (2010) Land Lines article (seven recommendations); Lincoln/GWIPP Significant Features database, Residential Property Tax Relief Programs topic (current tables are JS-rendered, so the page would need either a manual read of the live tool or the 2018 summary xlsx as a dated anchor); state statutes and agency pages (Minnesota Revenue read; Michigan blocked, use Michigan statute or the Michigan.gov tax pages another way only if openly served). ITEP would be cited only as a 2026 tally and as an advocacy characterisation. Suggested slug concepts/property-tax-circuit-breaker.md.

Scanner premise errors: (a) 'ITEP never cited on the wiki before' is true, but 'at least six pages' use the term is false (four, one irrelevant). (b) Scanner says '19 of 29 target seniors only; 20 of 29 plus DC cover renters': these are the Key Findings figures, but the same report's body and appendix give 19 of 30 and 21 of 30, plus 'Eleven states' versus Key Findings '10 states and D.C.' for non-seniors, and Appendix A gives non-senior homeowner coverage 14/30. The tallies should not be quoted as a precise figure; use only '29 states and the District of Columbia' (stated consistently on p.2, p.6, Appendix A list) and 'a majority are seniors-only'. (c) Scanner says the report 'compared circuit breakers with ... rate caps': the report names 'tax rate caps' once (p.3) as a proposal type but its detailed comparison covers only homestead exemptions and assessment-growth caps; rate/levy caps are not analysed. (d) Scanner context says the report 'cites' landlord pass-through and racial equity: ITEP asserts both as 'widely understood' or 'research suggests' with citations only to Berry 2021 and Avenancio-Leon & Howard 2022 (QJE) for over-assessment of low-value and minority-owned homes, not for pass-through incidence; the pass-through is stated without a source, and the wiki should treat it as ITEP's assertion (the economics literature on property-tax incidence is more qualified). (e) 'Phase-outs' and 'share of rent deemed to be tax' are not specified by ITEP (no percentage; no general phase-out rule). (f) 'One in three households pays over 30 per cent': real, p.3, but unsourced in the report. (g) The report says 'As of 2025' for the count while the figures and appendix are dated 2026 and the page dated November 2026; the Fig.1 note says September 2026 on the page and November 2026 in the PDF. (h) Scanner calls it a 'mainstream' source; it is an advocacy think-tank with a stated policy preference (Tier 2), and its Key Finding that circuit breakers are 'states' best tools' is a policy conclusion.

Georgist relevance is indirect: the report never mentions land value taxation, deferral as a distinct tool (it lumps deferrals with other income-limited programmes it deems less targeted, p.5), or land-vs-building assessment. Its argument that circuit breakers leave the tax base intact is an inference for LVT mitigation, not a finding about LVT; any wiki prose must keep that boundary, and must not present the report as evidence that circuit breakers solve the LVT asset-rich/cash-poor problem. Also a design caution relevant to the objection page: ITEP says circuit-breaker credits need annual claims and have uptake gaps, which cuts against treating them as a complete answer; the wiki's Wyoming page already notes a 44 per cent application rate on an application-based exemption.

Figures with unchecked provenance: Appendix C (FY2022 costs, claims, average credits) are ITEP's compilations from Census of Governments and state reports; several states are 'n/a' including Michigan, and the Minnesota decile bars were read from extracted chart text. Not checked against the Minnesota 2026 Tax Incidence Study PDF (named in ITEP endnote 14, URL on revenue.state.mn.us, not fetched).

Date oddities: ITEP's Fig.1 source note cites 'September 2026' on the web page and 'November 2026' in the PDF, and the page also says counts are 'as of 2025'. Lincoln database currency: ITEP cites the database with 'Accessed May 1, 2026' and '2024 information'; Lincoln's own summary tables served openly are for 2018 and could not be used for a 2026 count. Hence the comparison 'ITEP 29+DC vs Lincoln' rests on 2008 (33+DC) and 2018 (30+DC) Lincoln counts only; the current Lincoln database count is unverified.
Michigan Treasury: one ordinary request returned 403; per access policy no retry or workaround. Michigan facts remain ITEP-sourced (B).
